t: ‘Smart’ Implants Are Driving Up Health Costs — Even When Patients Don’t Ask for Them

p: Steve Russak, 70, of Santa Rosa Valley, California, woke up from knee replacement surgery last year to a text message. It was from the company that made his new knee. Over the next few days, the company, Zimmer Biomet, texted four times. Russak didn’t understand the inquiries asking him to use an app, he said.
Finally, a company representative called and offered help setting up some accessories, Russak told KFF Health News. “I said, ‘What? I don’t know what you’re talking about.’”

It turned out Russak did not receive just any old replacement of bone and cartilage. He’d had a “smart knee” put in — an artificial joint called the Persona IQ with a lithium-ion battery, sensors, and transmitter that, should he authorize it, would send data about his gait and range of motion to his clinicians and Zimmer.
Russak is suing the doctor, Zimmer, and Canary Medical, a health technology company that helped develop the device.

, Russak claims the knee was an “unauthorized implantation” and that, according to Zimmer’s “patient-facing materials,” he should have been given the option to opt out of data collection or decline the knee altogether, but wasn’t.

Russak said he doesn’t want to set up the device to collect and transmit data for several reasons, including his privacy. Now that it’s in his body, though, he said it poses potential disruptions. For example, Russak said he recently couldn’t get an MRI because of compatibility issues.
Neither the doctor nor the doctor’s lawyer responded to multiple requests for comment.

The case is ongoing, with the next hearing scheduled for December. Russak said he has dropped the fraud and breach of fiduciary duty allegations originally filed against the doctor but is continuing to sue on other grounds, including lack of informed consent. The doctor has yet to respond to the complaint in court.
Both
and

filed initial responses denying “each and every allegation” in Russak’s complaint. They have offered a variety of defenses, including that any damages are the fault of another party or, as Zimmer’s response said, caused by actions or reactions “not reasonably foreseeable.”

Canary Medical did not respond to requests for comment. Zimmer spokesperson Troy Kirkpatrick declined to comment on lawsuits against the company but said that “nearly 90%” of surveyed patients who received Zimmer’s joint replacements report they would choose an orthopedic device with remote monitoring capabilities again in the future.

“The transmission of post-operative recovery data requires patient authorization at the time the patient sets up an account and is designed to support patient-surgeon relationships and postoperative care,” Kirkpatrick said in an emailed statement. He added that Zimmer takes privacy and compliance with regulations “very seriously.”

p: The smart knee is part of a burgeoning trend in American medicine. While Zimmer introduced its device as “

” FDA-approved smart knee in 2021, there’s now a range of internet-connected devices — from implants to external products such as blood pressure monitors — that report data about patients’ conditions to doctors or other medical professionals. To proponents, the products offer the chance for better care: They can provide measurements showing whether a patient’s glucose is swerving out of control, for instance.

However, enhanced monitoring comes with potential drawbacks, including threats to privacy, and some doctors and researchers caution there is little evidence that smart devices improve health outcomes.

There’s “a lot of enthusiasm for remote monitoring technologies. There is tremendous potential,” said Sanket Dhruva, a University of California-San Francisco cardiologist and digital health researcher. But there’s a need for more rigorous data, he said. “We’re getting all this data — is this helping our patients recover better? That’s what we really care about.” Nonetheless, such devices generally mean more money for doctors, who can charge to examine the information they collect.
Both Medicare and private insurers reimburse clinical professionals for reviewing data from smart devices. In 2024, nearly

received that service, known as “remote patient monitoring,” according to the Department of Health and Human Services’ Office of Inspector General. Medicare, the federal program covering older Americans and some with disabilities, paid medical providers $536 million for remote monitoring, more than double what it paid three years earlier. The watchdog also cautioned that companies sometimes cold-call patients to offer and sign them up for devices they may not need.

In the case of Zimmer, Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services spokesperson Christopher Krepich emailed KFF Health News that “CMS payment does not mean the agency endorses a manufacturer’s marketing claims or guarantees that a technology improves outcomes for every patient.” He said the agency regularly evaluates its reimbursement policies.

Russak’s Medicare account shows the program paid for his surgery and knee implant, but it has not received any claims related to remote monitoring for the device, which he has not set up to transmit data.

The smart knee is one of the flagship orthopedic products of Indiana-based Zimmer Biomet, which also manufactures non-connected knee joints. The company — which hired professional strongman, actor, and former California governor Arnold Schwarzenegger to pitch its products as its “chief movement officer” — sold some $3.3 billion in knee joints last year.

p: Up the California coast in Contra Costa County, Jodi Murphy filed a lawsuit against Zimmer, Canary Medical, and her doctor after receiving a Persona IQ knee implant and being registered to use Zimmer’s app. The

The doctor and her practice

The doctor did not respond to requests for comment. Murphy and her lawyer declined to comment.

Russak’s lawsuit alleges his doctor told him he “had not disclosed the electronic nature, wireless transmission functions, or data-collection capabilities of the Persona IQ to prior patients in whom he had implanted the same device.” It goes on to cite that exchange as evidence that the companies “failed to adequately educate” the doctor.
“I don’t believe that Zimmer or Canary are training the doctors, and it’s an issue,” Russak told KFF Health News.

Bozic said orthopedic surgeons he knows are “ambivalent” about Zimmer’s smart knee devices and many don’t use them. The implant is the “most generic part of the operation and really doesn’t have a big impact at all on the outcome.”

In theory, he said, the data collected by the device about the number of steps a patient takes and the joint’s range of motion makes for better care. If a patient becomes more sedentary, that could be a useful signal for clinicians, he said.
But, in practice, “it’s a nice-to-have, certainly not a need-to-have,” Bozic said, “certainly not something that I would want to add significant cost to the procedure for.”
Surgeons already check on patients and ask to be informed if their health changes, he said. “It’s overkill to have it in the knee.”

Smart-knee manufacturers have also profited from a different Medicare benefit — a “new technology add-on payment” — that effectively temporarily subsidizes the adoption of otherwise money-losing new devices, thereby encouraging innovation. (The extra payment for Persona IQ lapsed in fall 2024.)

The payment program has undergone several adjustments in recent years. Beginning in late 2020 — until the government adjusted the benefit this year — there was no requirement that new technology substantially improve on older devices or pills. That lack of a requirement, predictably, meant more qualifying therapies. A
found an average of four approved annually in the near decade before the 2020 change; in the next four fiscal years, the authors said, the average moved up to nearly 15 a year.

The subsidy has lasting benefits for the manufacturers, said Dhruva, the UCSF cardiologist, who studies digital technologies and reimbursement. Medicare’s reimbursements are based on the average costs of a procedure. Since the subsidy increases the cost of the procedure, it increases the average costs, too — thereby driving up the basis for future costs.
Indeed, Dhruva said, the problem of payments for unproven services is present in Medicare reimbursement for remote patient monitoring, too.

Dhruva said there is a dearth of evidence showing the value of remote monitoring generally and of smart knees in particular, though taxpayers have been subsidizing it. “In general, the field is in need of much more rigorous data.”
Then there are the privacy concerns — the implications of what happens when someone the patient doesn’t want to get the data does.

Overall, these devices are dealing with “quite a bit of data, and oftentimes the issue really crystallizes around patients’ not understanding the information collection, use, and disclosure,” said Kate Black, a health data privacy lawyer not involved with the Russak or Murphy cases.
Consent standards for devices such as a smart knee “should be quite high,” she said, because, unlike a wearable product, an implanted device stays in for years.
“Every step you take, they know every step you take,” Russak said.
